title: Part 2, Chapter 6
paragraphs: But as soon as she left, he got up, latched the door, unwrapped the bundle Razumihin had brought that evening and tied up again, and began dressing. Strangely, he seemed to have become perfectly calm all at once -- not a trace of his recent delirium or the panic that had haunted him lately. It was the first moment of a peculiar, sudden calm. His movements were precise and deliberate; a clear purpose was evident in them. "Today, today," he muttered to himself. He knew he was still weak, but a fierce inner concentration gave him strength and confidence. He hoped he would not collapse in the street. Once he had put on his entirely new clothes, he looked at the money on the table and, after a moment's thought, pocketed it. Twenty-five rubles. He also took the copper change left from the ten rubles Razumihin had spent on the clothes. Then he quietly unlatched the door, slipped out, crept downstairs, and glanced through the open kitchen door. Nastasya was standing with her back to him, stoking the landlady's samovar. She heard nothing. Who would have imagined he would go out? A minute later he was in the street.

It was nearly eight o'clock. The sun was setting. It was as stifling as before, but he drank in the foul, dusty city air eagerly. His head felt slightly dizzy. A savage energy suddenly gleamed in his feverish eyes and his wasted, pale, yellowish face. He did not know or think about where he was going. He had only one thought: "All of _this_ must end today, once and for all, right now. I will not go home without it, because I _will not go on living like this_." How would he end it? With what? He had no idea and did not even want to think about it. He pushed thought away -- thought was torture. All he knew, all he felt, was that everything must change "one way or another," he repeated with desperate, unshakable determination.

Out of old habit he took his usual route toward the Hay Market. A dark-haired young man with a barrel organ stood in the street outside a small general shop, grinding out a sentimental song. He was accompanying a girl of about fifteen who stood on the pavement in front of him. She was dressed in a crinoline, a cloak, and a straw hat with a flame-colored feather -- all old and shabby. In a strong, rather pleasant voice, roughened by street singing, she sang hoping for a coin from the shop. Raskolnikov stopped among the two or three listeners, took out a five-kopeck piece, and placed it in the girl's hand. She broke off abruptly on a sentimental high note, shouted "Come on" to the organ grinder, and they both moved on to the next shop.
"Do you like street music?" Raskolnikov asked, turning to a middle-aged man standing idly beside him. The man looked at him, startled and puzzled.

"I love hearing someone sing to a street organ," said Raskolnikov, and his manner seemed strangely disconnected from the subject. "I like it on cold, dark, damp autumn evenings -- they must be damp -- when all the passersby have pale green, sickly faces. Or better still when wet snow is falling straight down with no wind -- you know what I mean? -- and the streetlamps glow through it..."
"I do not know.... Excuse me..." the stranger muttered, unnerved by both the question and Raskolnikov's strange manner, and he crossed to the other side of the street.

Raskolnikov walked straight on and came to the corner of the Hay Market where the stallholder and his wife had spoken with Lizaveta. But they were not there now. Recognizing the spot, he stopped, looked around, and addressed a young fellow in a red shirt who was lounging outside a grain dealer's shop.
"Is there not a man who keeps a stall here with his wife, at this corner?"
"All sorts of people keep stalls here," the young man answered, looking down at Raskolnikov with condescension.
"What is his name?"
"Whatever he was christened."
"Are you not from Zaraisk yourself? Which province?"
The young man looked at Raskolnikov again.
"It is not a province, your excellency, it is a district. Forgive me graciously, your excellency!"
"Is that a tavern up there?"
"Yes, it is an eating house, and there is a billiard room, and you will find princesses there too.... La-la!"

Raskolnikov crossed the square. In that corner a dense crowd of peasants had gathered. He pushed his way into the thickest part, studying their faces. He felt an inexplicable urge to talk to people. But the peasants ignored him -- they were all shouting in clusters together. He stood there thinking for a moment, then turned right in the direction of V. Prospect.

He had often passed through that little street which angles off from the marketplace toward Sadovy Street. Lately he had often felt drawn to wander around this area whenever he was depressed, so that he might feel even worse.

Now he walked along thinking of nothing. Here there was a huge block of buildings, entirely given over to taverns and eating houses. Women were constantly running in and out -- bareheaded, in their house clothes. They gathered in groups here and there on the pavement, especially around the entrances to various establishments on the ground floor. From one of these came a loud racket -- singing, guitar, and shouts of merriment floating into the street. A crowd of women thronged around the door. Some sat on the steps, others on the pavement, others stood talking. A drunken soldier was staggering along the road nearby, smoking and swearing. He seemed to be trying to find his way somewhere but had forgotten where. One beggar was arguing with another, and a man dead drunk was lying across the road. Raskolnikov joined the group of women, who were talking in hoarse voices. They were bareheaded and wore cotton dresses and goatskin shoes. Some were about forty, others no more than seventeen. Nearly all had blackened eyes.

He felt strangely drawn by the singing and noise from the saloon below.... Someone inside was dancing with wild abandon, stamping his heels to the sounds of a guitar and a thin falsetto voice singing a lively tune. He listened intently, gloomily, dreamily, bending down at the entrance and peering in from the pavement.

"Oh, my handsome soldier,
Don't beat me for nothing,"
trilled the singer's thin voice. Raskolnikov felt a powerful urge to make out the words, as though everything depended on it.
"Should I go in?" he thought. "They are laughing. Drunk. Should I get drunk?"
"Will you not come in?" one of the women asked. Her voice was still musical, less hoarse than the others. She was young and not bad-looking -- the only one in the group.
"Why, she is pretty," he said, straightening up and looking at her.
She smiled, very pleased by the compliment.
"You are not bad looking yourself," she said.
"Is he not thin, though!" another woman observed in a deep voice. "Just come out of the hospital?"
"They all look like generals' daughters, but every one of them has a snub nose," a tipsy peasant in a loose coat chimed in with a sly grin. "Look how jolly they are."
"Get out of here!"
"I am going, sweetheart!"
And he ducked into the saloon below. Raskolnikov moved on.
"Hey, sir!" the girl called after him.
"What?"
She hesitated.
"I would always be happy to spend some time with you, kind sir, but right now I feel shy. Give me six kopecks for a drink, there is a nice young man!"
Raskolnikov gave her whatever came to hand first -- fifteen kopecks.
"Oh, what a generous gentleman!"
"What is your name?"
"Ask for Duclida."
"Well, that is too much," one of the other women remarked, shaking her head at Duclida. "I do not know how you can ask like that. I would die of shame...."

Raskolnikov looked curiously at the speaker. She was a pockmarked woman of about thirty, covered in bruises, with a swollen upper lip. She delivered her criticism quietly and earnestly. "Where is it," thought Raskolnikov, "where have I read about a man condemned to death who says or thinks, an hour before his execution, that if he had to live on some high rock, on such a narrow ledge that there was only room to stand, and all around was the ocean, eternal darkness, eternal solitude, eternal storms -- if he had to remain standing on a square yard of space for the rest of his life, a thousand years, an eternity -- it would still be better to live like that than to die right now! Only to live, to live and live! Life, whatever it may be!... How true that is! My God, how true! Man is a vile creature!... And vile is the one who calls him vile for that," he added a moment later.

He turned into another street. "The Palais de Cristal! Razumihin was just talking about the Palais de Cristal. But what was it I wanted? Yes, the newspapers.... Zossimov said he read about it in the papers. Do you have newspapers?" he asked, entering a fairly spacious and reasonably clean restaurant with several rooms that were, however, rather empty. Two or three people were drinking tea, and in a further room four men sat drinking champagne. Raskolnikov thought one of them might be Zametov, but he could not be sure at that distance. "What if it is?" he thought.
"Will you have vodka?" asked the waiter.
"Bring me tea, and the newspapers -- the old ones from the last five days -- and I will tip you."
"Yes, sir. Here is today's. No vodka?"
The old newspapers and tea were brought. Raskolnikov sat down and began scanning them.

"Oh, damn... news items. An accident on a staircase, spontaneous combustion of a shopkeeper from alcohol, a fire in Peski... a fire in the Petersburg district... another fire in the Petersburg district... and another fire in the Petersburg district.... Ah, here it is!" He found what he was looking for and began reading. The lines danced before his eyes, but he read it all and eagerly searched for later updates in the following issues. His hands trembled with nervous impatience as he turned the pages. Suddenly someone sat down at his table. He looked up. It was Zametov, the head clerk, looking just the same -- rings on his fingers, watch chain, curly black hair parted and pomaded, smart waistcoat, rather shabby coat, and somewhat questionable linen. He was in a good mood -- at least he was smiling quite cheerfully and good-naturedly. His dark face was slightly flushed from the champagne.
"What, you here?" he began in surprise, speaking as though they were old friends. "Razumihin told me only yesterday you were unconscious. How strange! And do you know I have been to see you?"
Raskolnikov knew he would come over. He set the papers aside and turned to Zametov. There was a smile on his lips, with a new shade of irritable impatience visible in it.

"I know you have," he answered. "I heard. You looked for my sock.... And you know Razumihin is mad about you? He says you have been with him to Luise Ivanovna's -- you know, the woman you tried to help, the one you winked about to the Lieutenant and he would not understand. Do you remember? How could he fail to understand? It was perfectly obvious."
"What a hothead he is!"
"The Lieutenant?"
"No, your friend Razumihin."
"You must lead a fine life, Mr. Zametov -- free admission to the most agreeable places. Who has been pouring champagne into you?"
"We just had... a drink together.... You talk about pouring!"

"A professional perk! You profit from everything!" Raskolnikov laughed. "It is all right, my dear boy," he added, slapping Zametov on the shoulder. "I am not saying it out of spite -- it is friendly, just for fun, as that workman of yours said when he was scuffling with Dmitri in the old woman case...."
"How do you know about that?"
"Maybe I know more about it than you do."
"How strange you are.... You must still be very ill. You should not have come out."
"Oh, do I seem strange to you?"
"Yes. What are you doing, reading the papers?"
"Yes."
"There is a lot about the fires."

"No, I am not reading about the fires." He looked mysteriously at Zametov, his lips twisting into a mocking smile. "No, I am not reading about the fires," he went on, winking at Zametov. "But confess, my dear fellow, you are dying to know what I am reading about."
"Not in the least. Can I not ask a question? Why do you keep--"
"Listen, you are a man of culture and education, yes?"
"I completed six years of gymnasium," Zametov said with some pride.

"Six years! Oh, my little sparrow! With your parting and your rings -- a man of means. Ha! What a charming boy!" Raskolnikov broke into a nervous laugh right in Zametov's face. Zametov drew back, more baffled than offended.
"How strange you are!" Zametov repeated seriously. "I cannot help thinking you are still delirious."
"Delirious? You are making that up, my little sparrow! So I am strange? You find me curious?"
"Yes, curious."
"Shall I tell you what I was reading, what I was searching for? Look how many papers I had them bring me. Suspicious, is it not?"
"Well, what is it?"
"Pricking up your ears?"
"What do you mean, 'pricking up my ears'?"

"I will explain later. But right now, my boy, I will declare to you... no, better: 'I confess'... No, that is not right either. 'I make a deposition and you take it.' I depose that I was reading, that I was searching -- and I came here specifically for this purpose -- for news about the murder of the old pawnbroker woman," he said in almost a whisper, bringing his face very close to Zametov's. Zametov stared at him, unmoving, without pulling away. What struck Zametov afterward as strangest of all was that the silence that followed lasted exactly a minute, and that they gazed at each other the whole time.
"What if you have been reading about it?" he exclaimed at last, confused and impatient. "What do I care? What of it?"

"The same old woman," Raskolnikov continued in the same whisper, ignoring Zametov's reaction, "the one you were all discussing at the police station, remember, when I fainted. Well, do you understand now?"
"What do you mean? Understand... what?" Zametov asked, almost alarmed.

Raskolnikov's tense, earnest expression was suddenly transformed, and he burst into the same nervous laugh as before, as though utterly unable to control himself. And in a flash he recalled with extraordinary vividness a moment from the recent past -- that moment when he stood behind the door with the axe, the latch trembling, the men outside cursing and shaking it, and he had felt a sudden urge to shout at them, to taunt them, to stick out his tongue, to mock them, to laugh, and laugh, and laugh!
"You are either mad, or..." Zametov began, then stopped, as though stunned by an idea that had suddenly flashed through his mind.
"Or? Or what? Go on, tell me!"
"Nothing," said Zametov, getting angry. "It is all nonsense!"

Both fell silent. After his sudden burst of laughter, Raskolnikov became abruptly thoughtful and melancholy. He put his elbow on the table and rested his head on his hand. He seemed to have completely forgotten about Zametov. The silence lasted some time.
"Why are you not drinking your tea? It is getting cold," said Zametov.

"What? Tea? Oh, yes...." Raskolnikov took a sip, put a morsel of bread in his mouth, and suddenly, looking at Zametov, seemed to remember everything. He pulled himself together. At the same instant his face resumed its original mocking expression. He went on drinking tea.

"There have been a lot of these crimes lately," Zametov said. "Just the other day I read in the Moscow News that a whole gang of counterfeiters was caught in Moscow. An entire organization. They were forging banknotes!"
"Oh, that was ages ago! I read about it a month ago," Raskolnikov answered calmly. "So you would call them criminals?" he added, smiling.
"Of course they are criminals."

"Them? They are children, amateurs, not criminals! Fifty people banding together for such a scheme -- what an idea! Three would be too many, and even then each would have to trust the others more than himself! One person gets drunk and blabs, and the whole thing collapses. Amateurs! They hired strangers to exchange the notes -- imagine entrusting something like that to a random person! And say these amateurs succeed and each makes a million -- then what? Each one depends on all the others for the rest of his life! Better to hang yourself right away! And they could not even exchange the notes properly. The man who went to the bank with five thousand -- his hands were shaking. He counted the first four thousand but did not bother counting the fifth -- he was in such a rush to stuff the money in his pocket and run. Obviously he aroused suspicion. And the whole thing fell apart because of one fool! Is that possible?"
"That his hands were shaking?" Zametov said. "Yes, that is quite possible. I am sure that is possible. Sometimes you just cannot handle the pressure."
"Handle that?"

"Could you handle it? No, I could not. For a hundred rubles, to go through such a terrifying experience? To walk into a bank with forged notes -- where spotting that sort of thing is their whole job? No, I would not have the nerve. Would you?"
Raskolnikov felt an intense urge to stick his tongue out again. Shivers kept running down his spine.

"Here is how I would do it," he began. "This is how I would exchange the notes. I would count the first thousand three or four times, forward and backward, examining each note. Then I would start on the second thousand, count halfway through, then hold up some fifty-ruble note to the light, turn it over, hold it to the light again -- to check if it was genuine. 'I am worried,' I would say, 'a relative of mine lost twenty-five rubles the other day because of a counterfeit note,' and I would tell them the whole story. Then after starting the third thousand, 'No, excuse me,' I would say, 'I think I miscounted the seventh hundred in the second batch,' and I would put down the third and go back to the second, and so on right through to the end. And when I was done, I would pull out a note from the fifth batch and one from the second, hold them to the light again, and ask doubtfully, 'Please exchange these,' and put the clerk in such a state that he would not know how to get rid of me. When I had finally left, I would come back. 'No, excuse me,' I would say, and ask for some clarification. That is how I would do it."

"What terrible things you say!" Zametov said, laughing. "But that is all just talk. In practice you would trip up, I bet. I believe that even a hardened, desperate man cannot always rely on himself, let alone you and me. Take a case close to home -- the old woman murdered in our district. The killer seemed like a desperate man, he risked everything in broad daylight, was saved by a miracle -- but his hands trembled too. He could not manage the robbery, he lost his nerve. That was obvious from the--"
Raskolnikov looked offended.
"Obvious? Then why do you not catch him?" he cried, taunting Zametov maliciously.
"Oh, they will catch him."

"Who? You? You think you could catch him? You have your work cut out! The big test for you people is whether a man is spending money or not. If he had nothing and suddenly starts spending, he must be the man. Any child could outsmart you that way."

"The fact is, that is exactly what they all do," Zametov answered. "A man commits a clever murder at the risk of his life and then goes straight to a tavern to spend the money. That is how they get caught. Not everyone is as clever as you. You would not go to a tavern, of course?"
Raskolnikov frowned and looked hard at Zametov.
"You seem to be enjoying this and would like to know how I would have acted in that case too?" he asked with displeasure.
"I would like to know," Zametov answered firmly and seriously. His words and his look began to take on an almost excessively earnest quality.
"Very much?"
"Very much!"

"All right then. Here is what I would have done," Raskolnikov began, bringing his face close to Zametov's again, staring at him again, speaking in a whisper again -- so that this time Zametov actually shuddered. "Here is what I would have done. I would have taken the money and jewels, walked straight out, and gone to some deserted place surrounded by fences where nobody ever goes -- a kitchen garden or something like that. I would have scouted it out beforehand -- some boulder weighing a hundred pounds or more that had been lying in the corner since the house was built. I would lift that boulder -- there would certainly be a hollow beneath it -- and put the money and jewelry in the hole. Then I would roll the stone back, press it down with my foot, and walk away. And for a year or two, maybe three, I would not touch it. And good luck finding it! Gone without a trace."

"You are a madman," Zametov said, and for some reason he too spoke in a whisper, and drew away from Raskolnikov, whose eyes were glittering. He had gone terribly pale, and his upper lip was trembling and quivering. He leaned as close as possible to Zametov, and his lips began to move without making a sound. This went on for half a minute. He knew what he was doing, but could not stop himself. The terrible word trembled on his lips, like the latch on that door -- another moment and it would break loose, another moment and he would let it go, he would speak.
"And what if it was I who murdered the old woman and Lizaveta?" he said suddenly -- and then realized what he had done.
Zametov stared at him wildly and turned as white as the tablecloth. His face contorted into a forced smile.
"But is that possible?" he managed to say faintly. Raskolnikov glared at him.
"Admit it -- you believed me, did you not?"
"Not at all! I believe it less than ever now," Zametov said hastily.
"Caught you, my little sparrow! So you _did_ believe it before, if now you believe it 'less than ever'?"
"Absolutely not!" cried Zametov, clearly flustered. "Have you been scaring me this whole time just to lead up to that?"

"So you do not believe it? Then what were you all whispering about behind my back when I left the police station? And why did the Lieutenant interrogate me after I fainted? Hey, waiter!" he called, standing up and grabbing his cap. "How much?"
"Thirty kopecks," the waiter replied, hurrying over.

"And here is twenty kopecks for vodka. Look at all this money!" He held out his trembling hand to Zametov, full of banknotes. "Red notes and blue -- twenty-five rubles. Where did I get them? And where did the new clothes come from? You know I did not have a kopeck. You have already cross-examined my landlady, I am sure.... Well, that is enough! _Assez cause!_ Until we meet again!"

He walked out trembling all over with a kind of wild, hysterical sensation that contained an element of unbearable ecstasy. Yet he was gloomy and desperately tired. His face was twisted as though after a seizure. His exhaustion was building rapidly. Any shock or irritation would instantly revive his energy, but his strength collapsed just as quickly once the stimulus was removed.

Zametov, left alone, sat for a long time in the same spot, lost in thought. Raskolnikov had unwittingly triggered a revolution in his brain on a certain point, helping him reach a definitive conclusion.
"Ilya Petrovitch is a blockhead," he decided.

Raskolnikov had barely stepped out of the restaurant when he bumped into Razumihin on the steps. They nearly collided before seeing each other. For a moment they stood staring. Razumihin was greatly taken aback, and then genuine anger blazed fiercely in his eyes.

"So here you are!" he shouted at the top of his voice. "You ran away from your bed! And I have been looking for you under the sofa! We even went up to the attic. I nearly beat Nastasya on your account. And here he is after all! Rodya! What is the meaning of this? Tell me the truth! Confess! Do you hear?"
"It means I am sick to death of all of you and I want to be alone," Raskolnikov answered calmly.
"Alone? When you can barely walk, when your face is white as a sheet and you are gasping for breath? Idiot!... What have you been doing in the Palais de Cristal? Out with it!"
"Let me go!" said Raskolnikov, trying to push past him. This was too much for Razumihin, who grabbed him firmly by the shoulder.
"Let you go? You dare tell me to let you go? Do you know what I will do? I will pick you up, tie you in a bundle, carry you home under my arm, and lock you in!"

"Listen, Razumihin," Raskolnikov began quietly, apparently calm. "Can you not see I do not want your charity? What kind of person takes pleasure in showering kindness on someone who... curses it, who finds it a burden? Why did you come looking for me at the start of my illness? Maybe I was perfectly happy to die. Did I not tell you plainly enough today that you are tormenting me, that I am... sick of you! You seem determined to torture people! I assure you that all of this is seriously hindering my recovery, because it constantly irritates me. You saw that Zossimov left earlier to avoid agitating me. You should leave me alone too, for God's sake! And what right do you have to hold me by force? Can you not see I am in full possession of my faculties? How, how can I convince you to stop persecuting me with your kindness? Call me ungrateful, call me vile -- just let me be, for God's sake, let me be! Let me be!"
He had begun calmly, savoring in advance the poisonous phrases he was about to deliver, but he finished panting and in a frenzy, just as he had been with Luzhin.
Razumihin stood for a moment, thought, and let his hand drop.

"Go to hell, then," he said quietly, almost reflectively. "Wait!" he bellowed, as Raskolnikov started to move. "Listen to me. Let me tell you that every one of you is a babbling, posturing fool! If you have the slightest trouble, you brood over it like a hen on an egg. And you are not even original about it! There is not a spark of independent life in any of you! You are made of candle wax and you have lymph instead of blood. I do not believe in a single one of you! In any situation, the first thing you all do is try to be as unlike a normal human being as possible! Wait!" he shouted with redoubled fury, noticing Raskolnikov was about to leave. "Hear me out! You know I am having a housewarming tonight. They have probably already arrived, but I left my uncle to host them -- I just ran over. And if you were not a fool, a complete and utter fool -- if you were an original instead of a translation... you see, Rodya, I admit you are clever, but you are a fool! -- if you were not a fool, you would come to my place tonight instead of wearing out your shoes in the streets! Since you have already gone out, there is nothing for it. I would give you a comfortable armchair -- my landlady has one... A cup of tea, some company.... Or you could lie on the sofa -- either way, you would be among us.... Zossimov will be there too. Will you come?"
"No."

"Rubbish!" Razumihin shouted, losing patience. "How can you know? You cannot answer for yourself! You do not understand these things.... I have fought and argued with people a thousand times and then gone running back to them.... You feel ashamed and you go back! So remember: Potchinkov's building, third floor...."
"Mr. Razumihin, I do believe you would let anyone beat you up, just out of sheer goodwill."
"Beat me? Who? Me? I would twist his nose off at the very thought! Potchinkov's building, number 47, Babushkin's apartment...."
"I am not coming, Razumihin." Raskolnikov turned and walked away.
"I bet you will!" Razumihin shouted after him. "I refuse to know you if you do not! Wait -- is Zametov in there?"
"Yes."
"Did you see him?"
"Yes."
"Talked to him?"
"Yes."
"What about? Never mind, do not tell me. Potchinkov's building, 47, Babushkin's place -- remember!"
Raskolnikov walked on and turned the corner into Sadovy Street. Razumihin watched him go, then waved his hand and went inside. But halfway up the stairs he stopped.

"Damn it," he muttered, almost aloud. "He sounds rational, and yet... I am a fool! Madmen can sound perfectly rational too! And that was exactly what Zossimov seemed afraid of." He tapped his forehead with his finger. "What if... how could I let him go off alone? He might drown himself.... What a blunder! I cannot allow it." And he ran back to catch Raskolnikov, but there was no sign of him. Cursing, he hurried back to the Palais de Cristal to find Zametov.

Raskolnikov walked straight to the X---- Bridge, stopped in the middle, leaned both elbows on the railing, and stared into the distance. Having parted from Razumihin, he felt so much weaker he could barely make it here. He longed to sit or lie down somewhere right there in the street. Leaning over the water, he gazed mechanically at the last pink flush of sunset, at the row of buildings darkening in the gathering twilight, at one distant attic window on the left bank that blazed as if on fire in the final rays, at the darkening water of the canal. The water seemed to hold his attention. Red circles finally flashed before his eyes; the buildings seemed to move, the passersby, the embankments, the carriages -- everything was spinning. Suddenly he flinched, saved perhaps from fainting by an eerie, horrifying sight. He noticed someone standing to his right. He looked and saw a tall woman in a kerchief, with a long, yellow, wasted face and red, sunken eyes. She was looking straight at him, but clearly saw nothing and recognized no one. Then she leaned her right hand on the railing, lifted her right leg over, then her left, and threw herself into the canal. The filthy water parted and swallowed its victim for a moment, but an instant later the drowning woman floated to the surface, drifting slowly with the current -- head and legs in the water, her skirt billowing over her back like a balloon.
"A woman drowning! A woman drowning!" dozens of voices shouted. People came running. Both banks filled with onlookers. On the bridge, people crowded around Raskolnikov, pressing in behind him.
"Lord have mercy! It is our Afrosinya!" a woman wailed tearfully nearby. "Lord have mercy! Someone save her! Pull her out, good people!"

"A boat! A boat!" came shouts from the crowd. But no boat was needed. A policeman ran down the steps to the canal, threw off his coat and boots, and plunged into the water. The rescue was easy: she had floated within two yards of the steps. He grabbed her clothes with his right hand and with his left seized a pole held out by a comrade. The drowning woman was hauled out immediately. They laid her on the granite pavement of the embankment. She soon regained consciousness, sat up, and began sneezing and coughing, stupidly wiping at her wet dress with her hands. She said nothing.

"She has drunk herself senseless," the same woman's voice wailed beside her. "Senseless. The other day she tried to hang herself and we cut her down. I had just run to the shop, left my girl to watch her -- and now look at this! She is a neighbor, sir, a neighbor -- we live close by, the second house from the end, right there...."

The crowd dispersed. The police remained around the woman. Someone mentioned the police station.... Raskolnikov watched it all with a strange feeling of indifference and detachment. He felt disgusted. "No, that is revolting... water... not good enough," he muttered to himself. "Nothing will come of it," he added. "Nothing to wait for. What about the police station...? And why is Zametov not at the station? It stays open until ten o'clock...." He turned his back to the railing and looked around.

"Very well then!" he said with sudden resolve. He moved away from the bridge and headed toward the police station. His heart felt hollow and empty. He did not want to think. Even his anguish had passed. There was no trace now of the energy with which he had set out "to make an end of it all." Total apathy had taken its place.

"Well, it is a way out," he thought, walking slowly and listlessly along the canal bank. "I will end it, at any rate, because I want to.... But is it a way out? What does it matter! There will be the square yard of space -- ha! But what an ending! Is it really the end? Should I tell them or not? Ah... to hell with it! I am so tired! If only I could sit or lie down somewhere! What I am most ashamed of is how stupid it all is. But I do not even care about that anymore! God, the idiotic ideas that come into one's head."

To reach the police station he had to go straight and take the second left. It was only a few steps away. But at the first corner he stopped, thought for a moment, then turned into a side street and went two blocks out of his way -- perhaps without any reason, or perhaps to delay a minute and buy time. He walked, staring at the ground. Suddenly someone seemed to whisper in his ear. He looked up and saw that he was standing at the very gate of _that_ house. He had not been near it, had not passed it, since _that_ evening. An overwhelming, inexplicable force drew him forward. He went through the gate, through the entrance, then into the first doorway on the right and started climbing the familiar staircase to the fourth floor. The narrow, steep staircase was very dark. He stopped on every landing and looked around curiously. On the first-floor landing the window frame had been removed. "That was not like that before," he thought. Here was the apartment on the second floor where Nikolay and Dmitri had been painting. "Shut up and the door freshly painted. It must be for rent." Then the third floor, and the fourth. "Here!" He was confused to find the door standing wide open. There were men inside; he could hear voices. He had not expected that. After a brief hesitation he climbed the last steps and entered. This apartment too was being renovated; there were workmen inside. This seemed to stun him. He had somehow expected to find everything exactly as he had left it -- perhaps even the corpses in the same positions on the floor. But now -- bare walls, no furniture. It felt wrong. He went to the window and sat on the sill. There were two workmen, both young, one much younger than the other. They were papering the walls with new white paper covered in lilac flowers, replacing the old dirty yellow wallpaper. For some reason, this annoyed Raskolnikov terribly. He glared at the new paper with distaste, as though it grieved him that everything had changed. The workmen had obviously stayed late and were now hurriedly rolling up their paper and preparing to leave. They paid no attention to Raskolnikov. They were talking. He folded his arms and listened.

"She comes to my place in the morning," the older one was telling the younger. "Crack of dawn, all dolled up. 'Why are you preening and primping?' says I. 'I am ready to do anything to please you, Tit Vassilitch!' she says. That is some behavior! And dressed up like a regular fashion magazine!"
"And what is a fashion magazine?" the younger one asked. He obviously looked up to the other as an authority.

"A fashion magazine is a bunch of pictures, colored ones, and they come to the tailors here every Saturday by mail from abroad, showing people how to dress -- men and women both. They are pictures. The men are usually wearing fur coats, and as for the ladies' getups -- well, they are beyond anything you can imagine."
"There is nothing you cannot find in Petersburg," the younger one exclaimed enthusiastically. "Except your mother and father, you can find everything!"
"Except those, you can find everything, my boy," the older one declared sententiously.

Raskolnikov got up and walked into the other room -- the one where the strongbox, the bed, and the chest of drawers had been. Without furniture, the room seemed tiny. The wallpaper was the same. In the corner you could see where the icon case had hung. He looked at the spot and went back to the window. The older workman eyed him sideways.
"What do you want?" he asked suddenly.

Instead of answering, Raskolnikov went out to the landing and pulled the doorbell. The same bell, the same tinny, cracked sound. He rang it a second time, and a third. He listened and remembered. The hideous, agonizing terror he had felt then began coming back with increasing vividness. He shuddered with each ring, and it gave him more and more satisfaction.
"Well, what do you want? Who are you?" the workman shouted, coming out to him. Raskolnikov went back inside.
"I want to rent a flat," he said. "I am looking around."
"People do not come looking at flats at night! And you should come with the building manager."
"They washed the floors -- will they paint them?" Raskolnikov went on. "Is there no blood?"
"What blood?"
"An old woman and her sister were murdered here. There was an enormous pool of it."
"What kind of man are you?" the workman cried, uneasy.
"What kind of man am I?"
"Yes."
"Want to find out? Come to the police station -- I will tell you there."
The workmen stared at him in amazement.
"It is time for us to go, we are late. Come on, Alyoshka. We need to lock up," said the older one.
"Fine, let us go," Raskolnikov said indifferently, and went out first, slowly descending the stairs. "Hey, building manager!" he called out in the gateway.
Several people were standing at the entrance, watching passersby -- the two building managers, a peasant woman, a man in a long coat, and a few others. Raskolnikov walked straight up to them.
"What do you want?" one of the managers asked.
"Have you been to the police station?"
"I was just there. What do you need?"
"Is it open?"
"Of course."
"Is the assistant there?"
"He was, for a while. What do you need?"
Raskolnikov made no reply. He stood among them, lost in thought.
"He came up to look at the apartment," the older workman said, stepping forward.
"Which apartment?"

"The one where we are working. 'Why did you wash away the blood?' he asks. 'There was a murder here,' he says, 'and I have come to rent it.' Then he started ringing the bell -- nearly broke it. 'Come to the police station,' he says, 'I will tell them everything.' Would not leave us alone."
The manager looked at Raskolnikov, frowning and confused.
"Who are you?" he demanded as impressively as he could.

"I am Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov, a former student. I live in Shil's building, not far from here, apartment number 14. Ask the building manager -- he knows me." Raskolnikov said all this in a lazy, dreamy voice, without turning around, staring intently into the darkening street.
"Why were you up in the apartment?"
"To look at it."
"What is there to look at?"
"Take him straight to the police station," the man in the long coat interjected abruptly.
Raskolnikov looked intently at him over his shoulder and said in the same slow, lazy tone:
"Let us go."
"Yes, take him!" the man continued, more boldly. "Why was he poking around up _there_? What has he got in mind, eh?"
"Not drunk, but God knows what is wrong with him," muttered the workman.
"But what do you want?" the manager shouted again, beginning to get genuinely angry. "Why are you hanging around?"
"Afraid of the police station, are you?" Raskolnikov said mockingly.
"Afraid? Why are you hanging around?"
"He is a crook!" the peasant woman shouted.
"Why waste time talking to him?" cried the other manager, a hulking peasant in an open coat with keys on his belt. "Get out of here! He is a crook, no doubt about it. Get going!"
And seizing Raskolnikov by the shoulder, he flung him into the street. He stumbled forward but caught his balance, looked silently at the spectators, and walked away.
"Strange fellow," the workman remarked.
"Strange people these days," said the woman.
"You should have taken him to the station anyway," the man in the long coat said.
"Better not to get involved," the big manager decided. "A born troublemaker! He _wants_ you to take him in -- once you do, you will never shake him off.... We know the type!"

"Should I go there or not?" thought Raskolnikov, standing in the middle of the road at the crossroads. He looked around, as though expecting someone to give him a decisive answer. But no sound came. Everything was dead and silent, like the stones he walked on -- dead to him, to him alone.... Suddenly, at the far end of the street, two hundred yards away in the gathering darkness, he saw a crowd and heard voices and shouts. In the middle of the crowd stood a carriage.... A light gleamed in the street. "What is it?" Raskolnikov turned right and walked toward the crowd. He seemed to be grasping at anything, and he smiled coldly when he recognized what was happening, for he had fully made up his mind to go to the police station and knew that it would all soon be over.
